demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette:
Michael, a 34-year-old school counselor, had always taken pride in his ability to remain calm in a crisis. That changed one afternoon when an eighth grader who had been threatening self-harm lunged for a pair of scissors on his desk. Acting on instinct, Michael grabbed the boy’s arm and pulled him back, but the student lost his footing and crashed head-first into the corner of a filing cabinet. The sound—a sickening crack—was followed by silence, then a seizure. Michael called 911, but the boy suffered a traumatic brain injury that required weeks of hospitalization. In the months that followed, Michael’s world narrowed to that single moment.

The memory did not fade. It came back fully—the smell of the room, the warmth of the boy’s arm, the crack—as if it were happening right now, across all his senses at once. Because the memory arrived with such force, Michael started noticing his heart pound at any sharp sound—a dropped tray in the cafeteria, a car backfiring—sounds that had never troubled him before, now felt like warnings. Yet when he tried to describe it, he could only produce fragments; the words would not come. The hospital’s antiseptic smell during a routine checkup plunged him back into that room, and he felt the same panic surge through his chest. After that appointment, Michael began calling ahead to schedule visits at times when the lobby was emptiest, and he would stand outside until the last possible moment—anything to avoid the smell and the memory it unleashed. Stress from work or a minor argument with his wife made his self-blame worse: he would think, “I should have done something differently. I destroyed his life—and mine.” The more he blamed himself, the more vivid the memory became, and each reliving confirmed that his life was finished. He began to doubt that he could ever make a good decision again. Because he had concluded that his own judgment could not be trusted, Michael felt that the only rational choice was to keep his mind constantly occupied — staying busy was the only way to avoid making another catastrophic mistake.

To survive, Michael kept his mind occupied all the time. He played podcasts while driving, listened to music during lunch, and stayed up late cleaning the garage. But the effort of maintaining this constant distraction exhausted him, and the memory would break through even stronger, leaving him shaking. His inability to stop the intrusions convinced him he was fundamentally broken. The fact that he still needed to work so hard to keep his mind occupied only confirmed that brokenness — a normal person would not have to fight this hard just to hold themselves together. He started avoiding the police station on his commute—taking a longer route—and that careful avoidance made him hypervigilant for any sign of a patrol car, so that a glimpse of a squad car became a trigger in itself. At night, he could not let himself fall asleep easily; he lay rigid, listening for sounds, alert to imagined danger. That hypervigilance drove him to find even more distractions before bed, but they only left him more on edge, and his body’s racing heart often brought the memory flooding back.

Over months, the pattern tightened. Every stress—a deadline, a phone call from the district—made his self-recrimination sharper, and sharper blame made him more sensitive to new stress, creating a loop he could not escape. He stopped telling his wife about his days because each time he tried to speak, the memory returned and he could not find the words. He took leave from work, hoping rest would help, but the emptiness only gave the memory more room. What frightened him most was the thought that if he ever let himself fully think about the event, he would fall apart completely. Yet the memory pushed through anyway, and each time it did, he felt the same overwhelming guilt, the same certainty that his life was destroyed.

Finally, his wife insisted he see someone. Michael agreed, but he came to the first session terrified: terrified that talking would make the memory worse, and terrified that nothing could ever make it better. He hoped someone might quiet the memory, but deep down he feared the memory would always feel like it was happening right now.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that a trigger directly leads to a maladaptive avoidance or distraction strategy; triggers are described as leading to memory, threat, or negative appraisals but not to strategies.
No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory creates or causes new triggers; instead, triggers are created by avoidance strategies or exist independently.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that a trigger directly leads to a maladaptive avoidance or distraction strategy; triggers are described as leading to memory, threat, or negative appraisals but not to strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory creates or causes new triggers; instead, triggers are created by avoidance strategies or exist independently.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where Michael's negative appraisals (e.g., self-blame, feeling broken) directly drive his maladaptive coping strategies (avoidance, distraction); instead, these strategies appear driven by the memory and threat.

The vignette does not show a causal relationship where Michael's maladaptive strategies (e.g., distraction, avoidance) directly worsen his negative appraisals; the strategies lead to memory breakthroughs which then fuel negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where Michael's negative appraisals (e.g., self-blame, feeling broken) directly drive his maladaptive coping strategies (avoidance, distraction); instead, these strategies appear driven by the memory and threat.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
